title: Αἴολος καὶ ἄνεμοι
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his tale at the Phaeacian court, comes to the floating island of Aeolus, whom Zeus has made keeper of the winds. Aeolus, who feasts all year with his six sons and the six daughters he has given them as wives, entertains him for a month and sends him off with a skin in which every wind but the West Wind is bound with a silver cord. Ten days out, with Ithaca in sight, Odysseus falls asleep at last; the crew, thinking the skin holds gold and silver from Aeolus, open it, and the winds carry the ships back to the island. When Odysseus returns to ask for help, Aeolus will not receive a man whom the gods hate and drives him away.

sentences.t: Αἰολίην δ’ ἐς νῆσον ἀφικόμεθ’·
sentences.tr: Aioliēn d’ es nēson aphikometh’·
sentences.l: And to the Aeolian island we came;
sentences.i: And we came to the Aeolian island;
sentences.n: The part opens inside Odysseus’s long tale at the Phaeacian court, which began at 9.2 and has no closing mark; the speeches inside it carry single quotation marks. Αἰολίην is the adjective ‘Aeolian’ with Ionic η (Attic Αἰολίαν), and the island is the home of Aeolus. ἀφικόμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive’, elided from ἀφικόμεθα. ἐς is Attic εἰς.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔναιεν
Αἴολος Ἱπποτάδης, φίλος ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν,
πλωτῇ ἐνὶ νήσῳ·
sentences.tr:
entha d’ enaien
Aiolos Hippotadēs, philos athanatoisi theoisin,
plōtēi eni nēsōi·
sentences.i: and there lived Aeolus, son of Hippotes, dear to the immortal gods, on a floating island;
sentences.n: Ἱπποτάδης is a patronymic in -άδης, ‘son of Hippotes’; its genitive Ἱπποτάδαο comes again at 36. ἔναιεν is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’. φίλος ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν is ‘dear to the immortal gods’, the dative naming those to whom he is dear; the dative ending -οισι is the Homeric one. πλωτῇ is ‘floating’, from πλέω; the ending -ῃ is the dative of the feminine adjective agreeing with νήσῳ.

sentences.t:
πᾶσαν δέ τέ μιν πέρι τεῖχος
χάλκεον ἄρρηκτον, λισσὴ δ’ ἀναδέδρομε πέτρη.
sentences.tr:
pasan de te min peri teichos
chalkeon arrēkton, lissē d’ anadedrome petrē.
sentences.l:
and the whole of it, round about, a wall
of bronze, unbreakable, and smooth rock has run up sheer.
sentences.i: and a wall of unbreakable bronze runs all round the whole of it, and smooth rock rises sheer.
sentences.n: No verb stands with τεῖχος: ‘there is a wall’ is understood. μιν is ‘it’, the island, and πᾶσαν agrees with it. πέρι is Attic περί with its accent thrown back because it follows the word it governs, μιν: ‘round it’. χάλκεον is ‘of bronze’ and ἄρρηκτον ‘unbreakable’ (ἀ- + ῥήγνυμι). ἀναδέδρομε is the perfect of ἀνατρέχω ‘run up’ with a present sense: the rock ‘has run up’, that is, stands up sheer. λισσός is ‘smooth’, with no handhold.

sentences.t:
τοῦ καὶ δώδεκα παῖδες ἐνὶ μεγάροις γεγάασιν,
ἓξ μὲν θυγατέρες, ἓξ δ’ υἱέες ἡβώοντες·
sentences.tr:
tou kai dōdeka paides eni megarois gegaasin,
hex men thygateres, hex d’ huiees hēbōontes·
sentences.l:
of him also twelve children in the halls have been born,
six daughters, and six sons in youthful vigour;
sentences.i: He has twelve children as well, born in his halls: six daughters and six sons in the vigour of youth;
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘of him, his’; the article-forms in Homer are often pronouns. γεγάασιν is the perfect of γίγνομαι, ‘have been born’, in the uncontracted epic form (Attic γεγόνασι). μεγάροις is the dative plural of μέγαρον ‘hall’. υἱέες is the older nominative plural (Attic υἱεῖς). ἡβώοντες is the participle of ἡβάω ‘be in the prime of youth’, with the lengthened vowel of epic (diectasis), from ἥβη ‘youth’. Line 6 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only with the first syllable of θυγατέρες lengthened, with the syllable before ἓξ counted long (ἓξ once began with a digamma), and with a spondee in the fifth foot (ἡβώοντες).

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε θυγατέρας πόρεν υἱάσιν εἶναι ἀκοίτις.
sentences.tr: enth’ ho ge thygateras poren huiasin einai akoitis.
sentences.l: there he his daughters gave to his sons to be wives.
sentences.i: There he gave his daughters to his sons to be their wives.
sentences.n: Homer states without comment that Aeolus married his daughters to his sons. πόρεν is the unaugmented aorist of πόρω ‘give, grant’; ὅ γε is ‘he, for his part’. υἱάσιν is the dative plural of υἱός from the old stem υἱ-, with -άσιν for Attic -οῖς. εἶναι with a dative is ‘to be (wives) for (his sons)’. ἀκοίτις is the accusative plural of ἄκοιτις ‘bedfellow, wife’, in -ις for -ιας. Line 7 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only with the first syllable of θυγατέρας lengthened and with εἶναι shortened before the vowel of ἀκοίτις.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἰεὶ παρὰ πατρὶ φίλῳ καὶ μητέρι κεδνῇ
δαίνυνται, παρὰ δέ σφιν ὀνείατα μυρία κεῖται,
κνισῆεν δέ τε δῶμα περιστεναχίζεται αὐλῇ
ἤματα·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aiei para patri philōi kai mēteri kednēi
dainyntai, para de sphin oneiata myria keitai,
knisēen de te dōma peristenachizetai aulēi
ēmata·
sentences.l:
And they always beside their dear father and trusty mother
feast, and beside them dainties numberless lie,
and the fat-scented house is made to echo all round in the courtyard
by day;
sentences.i: They are always feasting beside their dear father and trusty mother, with countless delicacies set out beside them, and all day long the house, rich with the smell of cooking fat, echoes all round in the courtyard;
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘they’, the twelve children: a pronoun, not the article. αἰεί is Attic ἀεί ‘always’. δαίνυνται ‘feast’ is the verb behind δαίς; κεδνῇ is ‘trusty’, the house rendering of κεδνός. ὀνείατα are ‘good things to eat’ and μυρία ‘countless’. κνισῆεν is ‘full of the savour of burning fat’, from κνίση. περιστεναχίζεται is a rare passive, ‘is made to echo all round’; αὐλῇ is the courtyard, and the picture is of the din of feasting filling house and court. ἤματα is an accusative of time, ‘by day’, set against νύκτας ‘by night’ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
νύκτας δ’ αὖτε παρ’ αἰδοίῃς ἀλόχοισιν
εὕδουσ’ ἔν τε τάπησι καὶ ἐν τρητοῖσι λέχεσσι.
sentences.tr:
nyktas d’ aute par’ aidoiēis alochoisin
heudous’ en te tapēsi kai en trētoisi lechessi.
sentences.l:
and by night in turn beside their revered wives
they sleep, both on rugs and on bored bedsteads.
sentences.i: and by night they sleep beside their revered wives, on rugs and on corded bedsteads.
sentences.n: νύκτας is an accusative of time, answering ἤματα. αὖτε is ‘in turn’. ἀλόχοισιν is the dative plural of ἄλοχος ‘wife’; αἰδοίῃς ‘revered’ has the short dative plural ending -ῃς, beside the longer -ῃσι. εὕδουσ’ is εὕδουσι elided, ‘they sleep’. ἔν τε … καὶ ἐν is ‘both on … and on’. τρητοῖσι is ‘bored’: the frame of the bed was pierced for the cords that held the bedding.

sentences.t: καὶ μὲν τῶν ἱκόμεσθα πόλιν καὶ δώματα καλά.
sentences.tr: kai men tōn hikomestha polin kai dōmata kala.
sentences.l: And indeed of them we reached the city and the fair halls.
sentences.i: And we came to their city and their fair halls.
sentences.n: τῶν is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘of them’, which English turns into ‘their’. ἱκόμεσθα is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’, with the epic ending -μεσθα for -μεθα. καὶ μέν is ‘and indeed’. πόλιν and δώματα are accusatives of the place reached, with no preposition. δώματα, plural of δῶμα, is ‘halls’.

sentences.t:
μῆνα δὲ πάντα φίλει με καὶ ἐξερέεινεν ἕκαστα,
Ἴλιον Ἀργείων τε νέας καὶ νόστον Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
mēna de panta philei me kai exereeinen hekasta,
Ilion Argeiōn te neas kai noston Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
And a whole month he treated me as a friend and was questioning me on each point,
Ilios and the ships of the Argives and the homecoming of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: And for a whole month he treated me as a friend and questioned me about every particular: about Ilios and the ships of the Argives and the homecoming of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: μῆνα is an accusative of duration, ‘for a month’. φίλει is the unaugmented imperfect of φιλέω, here ‘treat as a friend, entertain a guest’. ἐξερέεινεν is the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω ‘ask out, question closely’. ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’, and the second line says what the things were: Ἴλιον is Troy, νέας is the Ionic accusative plural of ναῦς ‘ship’, and νόστον is the ‘homecoming’. Argives and Achaeans are two of Homer’s names for the Greeks.

sentences.t: καὶ μὲν ἐγὼ τῷ πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν κατέλεξα.
sentences.tr: kai men egō tōi panta kata moiran katelexa.
sentences.l: And indeed I to him all things according to what is fitting recounted.
sentences.i: And I told him all of it, as was fitting.
sentences.n: κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘according to what is fitting’ (μοῖρα ‘portion, due’), the house rendering. κατέλεξα is the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount’. τῷ is ‘to him’, the article as a pronoun in the dative, and ἐγώ is stressed: Odysseus tells everything as Aeolus had asked.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ ἐγὼν ὁδὸν ᾔτεον ἠδ’ ἐκέλευον
πεμπέμεν, οὐδέ τι κεῖνος ἀνήνατο, τεῦχε δὲ πομπήν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kai egōn hodon ēiteon ēd’ ekeleuon
pempemen, oude ti keinos anēnato, teuche de pompēn.
sentences.l:
But when I, for my part, a journey asked for and urged him
to send me, not at all did he refuse, but prepared an escort.
sentences.i: But when I in my turn asked for a journey and urged him to send me on it, he did not refuse at all, and arranged my escort.
sentences.n: ἐγών is ἐγώ in epic. ᾔτεον and ἐκέλευον are imperfects, ‘was asking and urging’. πεμπέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, ‘to send’, and οὐδέ τι is ‘not at all’. ἀνήνατο is the aorist middle of ἀναίνομαι ‘refuse’. τεῦχε is the unaugmented imperfect of τεύχω ‘make, prepare’. πομπή is the escort that sends a guest on his way.

sentences.t:
δῶκε δέ μ’ ἐκδείρας ἀσκὸν βοὸς ἐννεώροιο,
ἔνθα δὲ βυκτάων ἀνέμων κατέδησε κέλευθα·
sentences.tr:
dōke de m’ ekdeiras askon boos enneōroio,
entha de byktaōn anemōn katedēse keleutha·
sentences.l:
And he gave me, having flayed it, a skin of a nine-year-old ox,
and there he bound down the ways of the roaring winds;
sentences.i: He flayed a nine-year-old ox and gave me the skin, and in it he bound down the ways of the roaring winds;
sentences.n: ἐκδείρας is the aorist participle of ἐκδέρω ‘flay’. ἀσκός is a skin used as a container, here a bag made of the whole hide, and βοὸς ἐννεώροιο is ‘of a nine-year-old ox’ (ἐννέωρος, ‘of nine seasons’). βυκτάων is a rare word, probably ‘blowing, roaring’, but its sense is not certain, and ‘roaring’ is the traditional guess. κέλευθα is the neuter plural ‘ways, paths’: the paths of the winds are tied up in the skin. κατέδησε is the aorist of καταδέω ‘bind down’, and ἔνθα is ‘there, in it’.

sentences.t:
κεῖνον γὰρ ταμίην ἀνέμων ποίησε Κρονίων,
ἠμὲν παυέμεναι ἠδ’ ὀρνύμεν, ὅν κ’ ἐθέλῃσι.
sentences.tr:
keinon gar tamiēn anemōn poiēse Kroniōn,
ēmen pauemenai ēd’ ornymen, hon k’ ethelēisi.
sentences.l:
for him steward of the winds had made the son of Cronus,
both to stop and to rouse up, whichever he may wish.
sentences.i: For the son of Cronus had made him steward of the winds, to calm or to rouse whichever wind he wished.
sentences.n: κεῖνον is epic and Ionic ἐκεῖνον ‘that man’, Aeolus. ταμίην is a second accusative: ‘had made him steward’. παυέμεναι and ὀρνύμεν are infinitives in -έμεναι and -μεν, ‘to stop’ and ‘to rouse’, tied by ἠμέν … ἠδέ ‘both … and’. ὅν κ’ ἐθέλῃσι is a general relative clause: κε with the subjunctive gives ‘whichever he may wish’. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘the son of Cronus’, that is Zeus.

sentences.t:
νηὶ δ’ ἐνὶ γλαφυρῇ κατέδει μέρμιθι φαεινῇ
ἀργυρέῃ, ἵνα μή τι παραπνεύσῃ ὀλίγον περ·
sentences.tr:
nēi d’ eni glaphyrēi katedei mermithi phaeinēi
argyreēi, hina mē ti parapneusēi oligon per·
sentences.l:
And in the hollow ship he was binding it down with a shining cord,
of silver, so that not at all anything might blow out past, even a little;
sentences.i: In the hollow ship he made it fast with a shining silver cord, so that not even the least breath could blow out past it;
sentences.n: κατέδει is the imperfect of καταδέω ‘bind down’, here a detail of how he made the skin fast; the skin is understood as the object. μέρμις is a ‘cord’, and ἀργυρέῃ ‘of silver’ follows φαεινῇ ‘shining’ with Ionic uncontracted -έῃ. ἵνα μή with the aorist subjunctive παραπνεύσῃ states a purpose negatively: ‘so that nothing should blow out past’. μή τι … ὀλίγον περ is ‘not anything, however little’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ πνοιὴν Ζεφύρου προέηκεν ἀῆναι,
ὄφρα φέροι νῆάς τε καὶ αὐτούς·
sentences.tr:
autar emoi pnoiēn Zephyrou proeēken aēnai,
ophra pheroi nēas te kai autous·
sentences.l:
but for me a breath of the West Wind he sent forth to blow,
that it might carry both the ships and ourselves;
sentences.i: But for me he sent forth a breath of the West Wind to blow, to carry both the ships and ourselves;
sentences.n: ἐμοί is a dative of advantage, ‘for me’. πνοιή is ‘a breath, a blowing’ (Attic πνοή), and Ζεφύρου is the genitive of Ζέφυρος ‘the West Wind’. προέηκεν is the aorist of προίημι ‘send forth’, and ἀῆναι the infinitive of ἄημι ‘blow’. ὄφρα with the optative φέροι expresses purpose after a past tense. αὐτούς is ‘the men themselves’, set against the ships.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλεν
ἐκτελέειν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ emellen
ekteleein·
sentences.l:
but not then was it going
to accomplish it;
sentences.i: but, as it turned out, it was not going to be accomplished;
sentences.n: ἄρ’ (ἄρα) marks what turned out to be so, as in οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες at 9.475. ἔμελλεν with an infinitive is ‘was going to’, and ἐκτελέειν, uncontracted, is ‘bring to completion’. No subject or object is expressed: what was not to be accomplished is the plan of the gift, and the next clause says why it failed.

sentences.t: αὐτῶν γὰρ ἀπωλόμεθ’ ἀφραδίῃσιν.
sentences.tr: autōn gar apōlometh’ aphradiēisin.
sentences.l: for by our very own follies we perished.
sentences.i: For we perished through our own folly.
sentences.n: The line echoes the poem’s opening statement at 1.7, αὐτῶν γὰρ σφετέρῃσιν ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ὄλοντο, that the companions perished through their own follies. αὐτῶν is the genitive of αὐτός ‘of ourselves’, giving ‘our own’. ἀφραδίῃσιν is the dative plural of ἀφραδίη ‘thoughtlessness, folly’; the dative of cause is in -ῃσιν. ἀπωλόμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι ‘perish’, elided from ἀπωλόμεθα.

sentences.t:
ἐννῆμαρ μὲν ὁμῶς πλέομεν νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ,
τῇ δεκάτῃ δ’ ἤδη ἀνεφαίνετο πατρὶς ἄρουρα,
καὶ δὴ πυρπολέοντας ἐλεύσσομεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντες·
sentences.tr:
ennēmar men homōs pleomen nyktas te kai ēmar,
tēi dekatēi d’ ēdē anephaineto patris aroura,
kai dē pyrpoleontas eleussomen engys eontes·
sentences.i: For nine days and nights together we sailed on, and by the tenth our native soil was coming into view, and we were so near that we could see men tending fires;
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ is an adverb, ‘for nine days’, and τῇ δεκάτῃ ‘on the tenth’ a dative of time. πατρὶς ἄρουρα is the fatherland’s soil, that is Ithaca, which is not named here; ἀνεφαίνετο is the imperfect middle of ἀναφαίνω ‘show up, appear’. πυρπολέοντας is the participle of πυρπολέω ‘tend fires’, uncontracted (Attic πυρπολοῦντας). ἐλεύσσομεν is ‘we were seeing’, and ἐόντες is the epic participle of εἰμί: ‘being near’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐμὲ μὲν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἐπήλυθε κεκμηῶτα,
αἰεὶ γὰρ πόδα νηὸς ἐνώμων, οὐδέ τῳ ἄλλῳ
δῶχ’ ἑτάρων, ἵνα θᾶσσον ἱκοίμεθα πατρίδα γαῖαν·
sentences.tr:
enth’ eme men glykys hypnos epēlythe kekmēōta,
aiei gar poda nēos enōmōn, oude tōi allōi
dōch’ hetarōn, hina thasson hikoimetha patrida gaian·
sentences.i: Then sweet sleep came upon me, worn out as I was; for I had always been handling the ship’s sheet, and had given it to no other of my companions, so that we might reach our fatherland the sooner;
sentences.n: ἐμὲ μέν is ‘me, for my part’, set against οἱ δ’ ἕταροι in the next unit. ἐπήλυθε is the epic aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come upon’, and κεκμηῶτα the perfect participle of κάμνω, ‘worn out’, in the epic form for Attic κεκμηκότα. πόδα is literally ‘foot’, here the sheet, the rope that sets the sail; Odysseus has held it himself. ἐνώμων is the imperfect of νωμάω ‘handle’. δῶχ’ is δῶκα, the aorist of δίδωμι, with κ turned to χ before the rough breathing of ἑτάρων. ἵνα with the optative ἱκοίμεθα gives purpose, and θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, ‘more quickly’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἕταροι ἐπέεσσι πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
καί μ’ ἔφασαν χρυσόν τε καὶ ἄργυρον οἴκαδ’ ἄγεσθαι
δῶρα παρ’ Αἰόλου μεγαλήτορος Ἱπποτάδαο.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hetaroi epeessi pros allēlous agoreuon,
kai m’ ephasan chryson te kai argyron oikad’ agesthai
dōra par’ Aiolou megalētoros Hippotadao.
sentences.l:
but my companions with words to one another were speaking,
and said that I gold and silver homeward was carrying off for myself,
gifts from Aeolus great-spirited, Hippotes’ son.
sentences.i: But my companions were speaking to one another, and said that I was taking home gold and silver, gifts from great-spirited Aeolus, the son of Hippotes.
sentences.n: ἕταροι is a by-form of ἑταῖροι ‘companions’. ἀγόρευον is ‘were speaking’, with ἐπέεσσι ‘with words’ (dative in -εσσι) and πρὸς ἀλλήλους ‘to one another’. καί μ’ ἔφασαν … ἄγεσθαι is ‘and said that I was taking’: ἔφασαν takes an accusative and infinitive, and the middle ἄγεσθαι is ‘carry off for oneself’. οἴκαδ’ is ‘homeward’, with -δε of direction. δῶρα is ‘gifts’, in apposition to ‘gold and silver’. μεγαλήτορος is the house ‘great-spirited’, and Ἱπποτάδαο has the genitive in -αο, Attic -ου. Line 36 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only with the ο of Αἰόλου lengthened.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipesken idōn es plēsion allon·
sentences.l: And thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: And as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: εἴπεσκεν has the suffix -σκ-, which makes a verb iterative: each time, ‘would say’. τις is ‘someone’, so one after another. ἰδών ‘looking’ is an aorist participle. ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον is ‘to another close by’. The unit ends at · because the men’s words follow; the same line stands at 8.328, where it introduces the words of the gods, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
ὦ πόποι, ὡς ὅδε πᾶσι φίλος καὶ τίμιός ἐστιν
ἀνθρώποις, ὅτεών τε πόλιν καὶ γαῖαν ἵκηται.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, hōs hode pasi philos kai timios estin
anthrōpois, hoteōn te polin kai gaian hikētai.
sentences.l:
‘Ah, how this man is to all both dear and honoured
to men, of whomever both city and land he may reach.
sentences.i: ‘Ah, how dear and how honoured this man is to everyone, whatever people’s city and land he comes to.
sentences.n: The companions’ words begin here; Murray prints no quotation marks. ὢ πόποι is the exclamation, the house ‘Ah’, here with envy in it. ὅδε ‘this man’ is Odysseus, asleep. πᾶσι belongs with ἀνθρώποις ‘to all men’, and τίμιος is ‘held in honour’. ὅτεών is the Ionic genitive plural of ὅστις, ‘of whatever people’, depending on πόλιν καὶ γαῖαν ‘city and land’. ἵκηται is the subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι in a general clause, ‘whenever he comes’.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ μὲν ἐκ Τροίης ἄγεται κειμήλια καλὰ
ληίδος, ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖτε ὁμὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτελέσαντες
οἴκαδε νισσόμεθα κενεὰς σὺν χεῖρας ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
polla men ek Troiēs agetai keimēlia kala
lēidos, hēmeis d’ aute homēn hodon ektelesantes
oikade nissometha keneas syn cheiras echontes·
sentences.i: He is bringing home many fair treasures from Troy, part of the booty, while we, who have finished the same journey, are going home with empty hands;
sentences.n: ἄγεται is the middle ‘carry off for oneself’. ληίδος is a genitive of the source, ‘out of the booty’. κειμήλια are ‘treasures’, things laid up (κεῖμαι). ἡμεῖς δ’ αὖτε is ‘but we, on the other side’, and ὁμήν is the feminine of ὁμός ‘same’: ‘the same road’. νισσόμεθα is ‘we are going’, the epic present of νίσσομαι. κενεάς is the Ionic accusative plural of κενός ‘empty’, and σὺν … ἔχοντες is ‘having along with us’, with χεῖρας as object. Line 42 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only with the final syllable of νισσόμεθα lengthened.

sentences.t:
καὶ νῦν οἱ τάδ’ ἔδωκε χαριζόμενος φιλότητι
Αἴολος.
sentences.tr:
kai nyn hoi tad’ edōke charizomenos philotēti
Aiolos.
sentences.l:
and now to him these things gave, doing a favour in friendship,
Aeolus.
sentences.i: And now Aeolus has given him these things as a favour, out of friendship.
sentences.n: οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘to him’, Odysseus. The name Αἴολος is held back to the start of line 44, the last word of the sentence. χαριζόμενος is ‘doing a favour, gratifying’, and φιλότητι ‘out of friendship’ is a dative of cause (φιλότης also means ‘love’).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε θᾶσσον ἰδώμεθα ὅττι τάδ’ ἐστίν,
ὅσσος τις χρυσός τε καὶ ἄργυρος ἀσκῷ ἔνεστιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ age thasson idōmetha hotti tad’ estin,
hossos tis chrysos te kai argyros askōi enestin.
sentences.l:
But come, more quickly let us see what these things are,
how much gold and silver in the skin there is.’
sentences.i: But come, let us quickly see what this is, how much gold and silver is in the skin.’
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, an urging phrase. ἰδώμεθα is the aorist middle subjunctive of ὁράω (stem ἰδ-), a hortative ‘let us see’. ὅττι is epic for ὅ τι ‘what’, introducing an indirect question, and ὅσσος τις is ‘how much’. ἀσκῷ ἔνεστιν is ‘is in the skin’; the speakers do not know that it holds winds. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφασαν, βουλὴ δὲ κακὴ νίκησεν ἑταίρων·
sentences.tr: hōs ephasan, boulē de kakē nikēsen hetairōn·
sentences.l: So they spoke, and counsel evil prevailed of the companions;
sentences.i: So they spoke, and the evil counsel of my companions won out;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφασαν is ‘So they spoke’, the plural of the house ὣς φάτο, and it closes the speech. νίκησεν is ‘won, prevailed’. βουλή is the plan to open the skin; the genitive ἑταίρων tells whose counsel it was, and Odysseus, asleep, has no say in it.

sentences.t: ἀσκὸν μὲν λῦσαν, ἄνεμοι δ’ ἐκ πάντες ὄρουσαν.
sentences.tr: askon men lysan, anemoi d’ ek pantes orousan.
sentences.l: The skin they loosed, and the winds out all rushed;
sentences.i: They loosed the skin, and all the winds rushed out.
sentences.n: λῦσαν is the unaugmented 3 pl. aorist of λύω ‘loose’ (Attic ἔλυσαν). ἐκ … ὄρουσαν is tmesis: the preverb ἐκ stands apart from the verb, which is the unaugmented aorist of ὀρούω ‘leap, rush’ (Attic ὤρουσαν). The winds, shut up in the skin, come out together (πάντες).

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ αἶψ’ ἁρπάξασα φέρεν πόντονδε θύελλα
κλαίοντας, γαίης ἄπο πατρίδος.
sentences.tr:
tous d’ aips’ harpaxasa pheren pontonde thyella
klaiontas, gaiēs apo patridos.
sentences.l:
And them at once, having snatched them up, was carrying to the open-sea a storm-blast,
weeping, away from their fatherland.
sentences.i: At once a storm-blast snatched them up and carried them out to the open sea, weeping, away from their fatherland.
sentences.n: τοὺς is ‘them’, the men, taken up again by κλαίοντας ‘weeping’. ἁρπάξασα is the aorist participle of ἁρπάζω ‘snatch’, and φέρεν the unaugmented imperfect ‘was carrying’. πόντονδε is ‘to the open sea’, with -δε of direction. θύελλα, the subject, is kept to the end of the line, the ‘storm-blast’. γαίης ἄπο is ‘away from the land’, with the preposition after its noun, and πατρίδος is the adjective ‘of the fathers’: the fatherland.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε
ἐγρόμενος κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονα μερμήριξα,
ἠὲ πεσὼν ἐκ νηὸς ἀποφθίμην ἐνὶ πόντῳ,
ἦ ἀκέων τλαίην καὶ ἔτι ζωοῖσι μετείην.
sentences.tr:
autar egō ge
egromenos kata thymon amymona mermērixa,
ēe pesōn ek nēos apophthimēn eni pontōi,
ē akeōn tlaiēn kai eti zōoisi meteiēn.
sentences.l:
but I,
waking, in my blameless heart pondered,
whether, having fallen from the ship, I should perish in the open-sea,
or in silence endure and still be among the living.
sentences.i: But I woke, and in my blameless heart I wondered whether to fall from the ship and perish in the open sea, or to endure in silence and remain among the living.
sentences.n: ἐγρόμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐγείρω, ‘having woken’. ἀμύμονα is the house ‘blameless’, though the word’s real sense is not known; it is translated even where it sits oddly, as of a heart. μερμήριξα is the aorist of μερμηρίζω ‘be torn in mind, ponder’. The two choices are optatives, ἀποφθίμην ‘I should perish’ and τλαίην ‘I should endure’, in a deliberative question, ‘whether … or’ (ἠέ … ἦ). ἀκέων is ‘in silence’, and ζωοῖσι the dative plural of ζωός (Attic ζῶσι), with μετείην ‘be among’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτλην καὶ ἔμεινα, καλυψάμενος δ’ ἐνὶ νηὶ
κείμην.
sentences.tr:
all’ etlēn kai emeina, kalypsamenos d’ eni nēi
keimēn.
sentences.l:
But I endured and stayed, and having covered myself in the ship
I lay.
sentences.i: But I endured and stayed, and lay covered up in the ship.
sentences.n: ἔτλην is the aorist of τλάω ‘endure’, and ἔμεινα ‘I stayed’ is the answer to the two choices of the line before: he does not throw himself overboard. καλυψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of καλύπτω, ‘having covered himself’. κείμην is the imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἐφέροντο κακῇ ἀνέμοιο θυέλλῃ
αὖτις ἐπ’ Αἰολίην νῆσον, στενάχοντο δ’ ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ epheronto kakēi anemoio thyellēi
autis ep’ Aioliēn nēson, stenachonto d’ hetairoi.
sentences.l:
and they were carried by an evil storm-blast of wind
again to the Aeolian island, and groaned the companions.
sentences.i: and the ships were carried by the evil storm-blast of the wind back to the Aeolian island, while my companions groaned.
sentences.n: αἱ is ‘they’, feminine plural, the ships of 26. ἐφέροντο is the passive imperfect, ‘were being carried’, and the dative κακῇ ἀνέμοιο θυέλλῃ is a dative of means, ‘by an evil storm-blast of wind’, with the genitive in -οιο. αὖτις is ‘again, back’. στενάχοντο is the imperfect of στενάχομαι ‘groan’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἐπ’ ἠπείρου βῆμεν καὶ ἀφυσσάμεθ’ ὕδωρ,
αἶψα δὲ δεῖπνον ἕλοντο θοῇς παρὰ νηυσὶν ἑταῖροι.
sentences.tr:
entha d’ ep’ ēpeirou bēmen kai aphyssameth’ hydōr,
aipsa de deipnon helonto thoēis para nēusin hetairoi.
sentences.l:
And there onto the mainland we went and drew water,
and quickly a meal took, by the swift ships, the companions.
sentences.i: There we went up onto the mainland and drew water, and my companions quickly took their meal beside the swift ships.
sentences.n: These two lines are the same as 9.85–86, and their English is kept. βῆμεν is an old aorist of βαίνω, ‘we went’. ἠπείρου is the mainland, over against the sea. ἀφυσσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἀφύσσω ‘draw’, the verb used of liquids. δεῖπνον ἕλοντο is ‘took a meal’, the aorist middle of αἱρέω. In θοῇς παρὰ νηυσίν the preposition stands between adjective and noun.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σίτοιό τ’ ἐπασσάμεθ’ ἠδὲ ποτῆτος,
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼ κήρυκά τ’ ὀπασσάμενος καὶ ἑταῖρον
βῆν εἰς Αἰόλου κλυτὰ δώματα·
sentences.tr:
autar epei sitoio t’ epassameth’ ēde potētos,
dē tot’ egō kēryka t’ opassamenos kai hetairon
bēn eis Aiolou klyta dōmata·
sentences.i: But when we had partaken of food and drink, I took a herald and a companion with me and went to the famous halls of Aeolus;
sentences.n: The first line is as at 9.87, and its English is kept. ἐπασσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of πατέομαι ‘partake of’, with the genitives σίτοιο and ποτῆτος. ὀπασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ὀπάζω, ‘take as attendant’; the herald and the companion are one man each. βῆν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, ‘I went’, here a short form for ἔβην. κλυτά is the house ‘famous’, and Αἰόλου is the genitive. Line 60 is metrically irregular as transmitted: it scans only with the ο of Αἰόλου lengthened.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐκίχανον
δαινύμενον παρὰ ᾗ τ’ ἀλόχῳ καὶ οἷσι τέκεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ekichanon
dainymenon para hēi t’ alochōi kai hoisi tekessin.
sentences.l:
and him I came upon
feasting beside his own wife and his own children.
sentences.i: and I found him feasting with his own wife and children.
sentences.n: ἐκίχανον is the imperfect of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’. δαινύμενον ‘feasting’ agrees with τόν ‘him’, the article as a pronoun, and echoes δαίνυνται at 9. ᾗ and οἷσι are the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, ‘his own’, easily mistaken for the relative: ‘his own wife and his own children’. τέκεσσιν is the dative plural of τέκος ‘child’, in -εσσιν.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δ’ ἐς δῶμα παρὰ σταθμοῖσιν ἐπ’ οὐδοῦ
ἑζόμεθ’·
sentences.tr:
elthontes d’ es dōma para stathmoisin ep’ oudou
hezometh’·
sentences.l:
And having come into the house, beside the doorposts, on the threshold,
we sat down;
sentences.i: We went into the house and sat down on the threshold by the doorposts;
sentences.n: ἐλθόντες is ‘having come’ and ἐς is Attic εἰς. σταθμοῖσιν is the dative plural of σταθμός ‘doorpost’, in -οισιν. ἑζόμεθ’ is ἑζόμεθα, the imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’; the party sits at the threshold, inside the house but not yet at the table.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἀνὰ θυμὸν ἐθάμβεον ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο·
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ana thymon ethambeon ek t’ ereonto·
sentences.l: and they in their heart were amazed and were asking questions:
sentences.i: They were amazed in their hearts, and asked:
sentences.n: οἱ is ‘they’, Aeolus and his family. ἐθάμβεον is the uncontracted imperfect of θαμβέω ‘be amazed’ (Attic ἐθάμβουν), and ἀνὰ θυμόν is ‘in their heart’. ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο is tmesis for ἐξερέοντο, from ἐξερέομαι ‘ask out, question’. The · leads into the words that follow.

sentences.t: πῶς ἦλθες, Ὀδυσεῦ;
sentences.tr: pōs ēlthes, Odyseu;
sentences.l: ‘How did you come, Odysseus?
sentences.i: ‘How have you come, Odysseus?
sentences.n: The household speaks; Murray prints no quotation marks, and the speech runs to the end of 66. Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς with a single σ, as Ὀδυσῆος stands beside Ὀδυσσῆος: the verse takes either. ἦλθες is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. It is a question, not a greeting: they had sent him off, and here he is.

sentences.t: τίς τοι κακὸς ἔχραε δαίμων;
sentences.tr: tis toi kakos echrae daimōn;
sentences.l: What evil power attacked you?
sentences.i: What evil power has set upon you?
sentences.n: τίς … δαίμων is ‘what power’; δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, the house ‘power’, and κακός ‘evil’ makes it hostile. τοι is the enclitic dative ‘to you’ (= σοι). ἔχραε is the imperfect of χράω ‘assail, attack’, in the uncontracted form.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν σ’ ἐνδυκέως ἀπεπέμπομεν, ὄφρ’ ἀφίκοιο
πατρίδα σὴν καὶ δῶμα καὶ εἴ πού τοι φίλον ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
ē men s’ endykeōs apepempomen, ophr’ aphikoio
patrida sēn kai dōma kai ei pou toi philon estin.
sentences.l:
Surely you kindly we were sending off, so that you might reach
your fatherland and house, and wherever it is dear to you.’
sentences.i: Surely we sent you off kindly, so that you might reach your fatherland and house, or wherever else is dear to you.’
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘surely, truly’, an emphatic pair. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly, with care’, and ἀπεπέμπομεν is the imperfect of ἀποπέμπω ‘send off’: ‘we were sending you off’. ὄφρα with the optative ἀφίκοιο gives purpose after a past tense. The words πατρίδα σὴν καὶ δῶμα … εἴ πού τοι φίλον ἐστίν are those of Alcinous’ promise at 7.320, and their English is kept; εἴ πού τοι φίλον ἐστίν is ‘if anywhere it is dear to you’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάσαν, αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μετεφώνεον ἀχνύμενος κῆρ·
sentences.tr: hōs phasan, autar egō metephōneon achnymenos kēr·
sentences.l: So they spoke, but I among them spoke, grieving in heart:
sentences.i: So they spoke, and I spoke among them, grieving in heart:
sentences.n: ὣς φάσαν is ‘So they spoke’, the plural of ὣς φάτο, with φάσαν the unaugmented imperfect of φημί (= ἔφασαν). μετεφώνεον is the uncontracted imperfect of μεταφωνέω ‘speak among’ (Attic μετεφώνουν). ἀχνύμενος is the middle participle of ἄχνυμαι ‘be grieved’, and κῆρ is an accusative of respect, ‘in heart’. Odysseus’s own words begin in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἄασάν μ’ ἕταροί τε κακοὶ πρὸς τοῖσί τε ὕπνος
σχέτλιος.
sentences.tr:
aasan m’ hetaroi te kakoi pros toisi te hypnos
schetlios.
sentences.l:
‘They blinded me, both base companions and, in addition to them, sleep,
cruel.
sentences.i: ‘My base companions blinded me, and cruel sleep as well.
sentences.n: ἄασάν is the aorist of ἀάω, ‘blind, delude, make go wrong in the mind’, the verb behind ἄτη ‘delusion’; the blindness is of the mind, not of the eyes. ἕταροί … κακοί is ‘base companions’. τε … τε is ‘both … and’, and πρὸς τοῖσι is ‘in addition to these’. σχέτλιος is the house ‘cruel’, and is held to the start of the next line, after ὕπνος.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀκέσασθε, φίλοι·
sentences.tr: all’ akesasthe, philoi·
sentences.l: But mend it, friends;
sentences.i: But set it right, friends;
sentences.n: ἀκέσασθε is the aorist middle imperative of ἀκέομαι ‘heal, mend’. The object is not given: it is the harm done. φίλοι is the vocative plural ‘friends’.

sentences.t: δύναμις γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν.
sentences.tr: dynamis gar en hymin.
sentences.l: for the power is in you.’
sentences.i: for the power lies with you.’
sentences.n: δύναμις is ‘power, ability’; the verb is understood (ἐστί), and ὑμῖν is the dative of ὑμεῖς ‘you (pl.)’. The speech ends here, with the appeal to Aeolus and his household.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην μαλακοῖσι καθαπτόμενος ἐπέεσσιν,
οἱ δ’ ἄνεῳ ἐγένοντο·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephamēn malakoisi kathaptomenos epeessin,
hoi d’ aneōi egenonto·
sentences.l:
So I spoke, with soft words accosting them,
but they fell speechless;
sentences.i: So I spoke, addressing them directly with soft words, and they fell speechless;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘So I spoke’, the first-person counterpart of ὣς φάτο, with ἐφάμην the imperfect middle of φημί. καθαπτόμενος ἐπέεσσιν is the house ‘accosting with words’, ‘addressing directly’, and μαλακοῖσι is ‘soft’ with the dative ending -οισι. ἄνεῳ is the plural of the adjective ‘speechless’, and ἐγένοντο is ‘became’: they fell speechless.

sentences.t: πατὴρ δ’ ἠμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: patēr d’ ēmeibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: but the father answered with a word:
sentences.i: but their father answered:
sentences.n: ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and μύθῳ is ‘with a word’. πατήρ is Aeolus, called by his place in the family rather than by name; at 8 his children feast beside their ‘dear father’. The unit ends at · because his words follow.

sentences.t: ἔρρ’ ἐκ νήσου θᾶσσον, ἐλέγχιστε ζωόντων·
sentences.tr: err’ ek nēsou thasson, elenchiste zōontōn·
sentences.l: ‘Begone from the island more quickly, most shameful of the living;
sentences.i: ‘Begone from the island, and quickly, you most shameful of the living;
sentences.n: Aeolus speaks; Murray prints no quotation marks, and the speech runs to the end of 75. ἔρρ’ is the imperative of ἔρρω ‘go away’, with a curse in it, the house ‘Begone’. θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς, ‘more quickly’, used as ‘quickly, at once’. ἐλέγχιστε is the vocative of ἐλέγχιστος, the superlative of the adjective ἐλεγχής ‘shameful’ (cf. ἔλεγχος ‘disgrace’): ‘most shameful’. ζωόντων is the genitive plural of the uncontracted participle of ζώω (Attic ζώντων): ‘of the living’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοι θέμις ἐστὶ κομιζέμεν οὐδ’ ἀποπέμπειν
ἄνδρα τόν, ὅς κε θεοῖσιν ἀπέχθηται μακάρεσσιν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar moi themis esti komizemen oud’ apopempein
andra ton, hos ke theoisin apechthētai makaressin·
sentences.l:
for not for me is it right to care for or to send off
that man who may become hateful to the blessed gods;
sentences.i: for it is not right for me to care for, or to send off, any man who has become hateful to the blessed gods;
sentences.n: θέμις ἐστί is ‘it is right’, by divine law. κομιζέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, ‘to care for, take in’, and ἀποπέμπειν ‘to send off’: he may not shelter Odysseus or give him an escort. ἄνδρα τόν is ‘that man’, the article as a demonstrative, and ὅς κε … ἀπέχθηται is a general clause, with κε and the aorist subjunctive of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful’, with the dative: ‘whoever becomes hateful to’. θεοῖσιν … μακάρεσσιν is ‘to the blessed gods’, in -οισιν and -εσσιν.

sentences.t: ἔρρε, ἐπεὶ ἄρα θεοῖσιν ἀπεχθόμενος τόδ’ ἱκάνεις.
sentences.tr: erre, epei ara theoisin apechthomenos tod’ hikaneis.
sentences.l: Begone, since then to the gods being hateful here you have come.’
sentences.i: Begone, since, as it appears, you come here hateful to the gods.’
sentences.n: ἔρρε repeats ἔρρ’ of 72, the house ‘Begone’, so that the speech begins and ends on the dismissal. ἐπεὶ ἄρα is ‘since, as it appears’: ἄρα marks the conclusion he draws from the storm. ἀπεχθόμενος is the participle of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘be hateful’, echoing ἀπέχθηται in 74. τόδ’ ἱκάνεις is ‘you come here’. The speech ends here.
